Bugatti CEO's Chiron Stolen With Keys Inside, Runs It Down in Porsche 911, Gets It Back Hours Later
24 photos
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike
The boss of Bugatti and Rimac isn’t your typical car nut. He built a hypercar empire from his dad’s garage, runs the greatest name in the automotive universe, and had 1,000% confidence in his conationals. So much so, that he didn’t even bother to lock his cars – or even take the keys with him. Until someone made off with his Chiron Sport.
Mate Rimac is probably the coolest car guy on the planet, bar none. He sits at the helm of not one, but two of the most formidable hypercar companies on Planet Speed – Bugatti and Rimac, in alphabetical order – and he rubs elbows with the likes of Christian von Koenigsegg, John Hennessey, Gordon Murray, as well as other, more obscure names in the business, like Porsche or BMW.
And he just had his car stolen. Remember that Batman movie line (with Val Kilmer playing Bruce Wayne): “He took the car!” “What car?” “The OTHER car!” Alfred was telling Batman that Robin had basically nicked the Batmobile. Well, Mate went through a very similar experience, with someone taking his Bugatti and crossing the border. You might want to crab popcorn for this one.
Better yet, pull up a barstool and order a cold pint, because the greatest automotive pub story of 2026 just dropped on Instagram courtesy of the man himself. A casual and regular reporter of his own adventures, Mate Rimac told it himself on Instagram.
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike Imagine being the 38-year-old chief executive of Bugatti Rimac and having your own personal hypercar nicked in broad daylight. From your own back yard. Literally. It sounds like the rejected script of a slapstick heist movie, yet on Wednesday, October 28, reality outshined fiction right outside of Zagreb, Croatia.
The machine at the center of this Balkan escapade is not a battered commuter hatchback, but Rimac’s personal Bugatti Chiron Sport, affectionately known by its Zagreb vanity plate moniker, CRO-BUG. Finished in dark blue exposed carbon fiber with a bold red number 16 on the horseshoe grille and Croatian tricolor flags under the wing mirrors, this 1-of-500 Molsheim masterpiece carried a casual market value of 3,000,000 euros, or $3,300,000.
The past tense is mandatory, because: A) the car is worth a lot more now, being Mate’s own ride, and B) it’s the only stolen Bugatti Chiron in the world that got recovered in less than 24 hours, and had the owner chase down the thief, accompanied by a multi-national police escort. (At this point, you’re wondering what car did Mate use to hunt a Chiron. Ironically, he actually does have something that will catch a Bugatti – the Rimac Nevera, remember? – but he went old-school. Read on).
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike Beneath that sculpted carbon skin sits an 8.0-liter quad-turbocharged W16 engine cranking out 1,500 PS, or 1,479 hp, and 1,600 Nm, or 1,180 lb-ft of torque. Tipping the scales at 1,978 kg, or 4,361 lbs, which is 18 kg, or 40 lbs, lighter than the standard model, the all-wheel-drive missile rockets from 0 to 100 kph, or 62 mph, in 2.4 seconds toward a 420-kph, or 261-mph, top speed.
Naturally, when you own a 1,500-PS hypercar that reaches 200 kph, or 124 mph, in 6.1 seconds and 300 kph, or 186 mph, in 13.1 seconds, you guard the keys with armed mercenaries, right? Not if you are Mate Rimac. For years, the company boss has casually left the keys sitting inside his Chiron and his Rimac Nevera, treating multi-million-euro engineering marvels like old farm tractors in a barn. Pardon the mistake. Like tractors outside the barn.
In his hilarious 6-minute Instagram confession, Rimac explained that he was simply proud of how safe Croatia is (he’s right to be proud, it’s a great country. Ask Elon Musk more details. Serbians, stay put). Furthermore, the sprawling Rimac Campus in Sveta Nedelja was deliberately designed without perimeter fences so visitors can walk right up to the buildings.
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike Because engineers and friends constantly borrow and test his cars while he sits in meetings, leaving the key fob inside saved everyone the daily hassle of chasing him around. And if someone with a bit of common sense will raise the question “Why can’t the keys stay in a basket in the lobby?”, good for you. Efficiency. Why waste time going to the keys and then to the car, when you can go straight to the car, and find the keys inside?
That utopian trust worked flawlessly until Wednesday afternoon, when a 36-year-old Croatian man strolled onto the unfenced campus looking for employment. That’s what Mate said the thief told him, once the whole adventure was over. Instead of dropping off a resume at the reception desk like a normal applicant, our ambitious protagonist spotted the 3,000,000-euro Bugatti parked outside with the key practically winking at him from the leather interior.
Skipping the interview entirely, he promoted himself to test pilot and rumbled right away. At this point, I have to give full credit to the man for two things: having the decency to put out his cigarette before climbing into 3.3 million bucks, and not damaging the driver seat with the enormous set of brass he was carrying. Mate posted a footage of the security cams - see it below. If this isn't going to be a chapter in GTA 6, they'd better not release it at all.
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike The funniest part of this Grand Theft Auto audition is that nobody at the factory would have noticed the car was missing for hours. Rimac admitted that so many colleagues drive his Chiron all the time that he rarely knows where it is on any given day. Only when a sharp-eyed bystander remarked that an unfamiliar bloke was piloting the blue beast did employees fire up a frantic internal group chat.
Once every executive and engineer confirmed they had not taken the W16 out for a coffee run, the comedy of errors turned into an international manhunt. If you are going to boost a car in 2026, stealing one from the man who engineers the world’s most advanced vehicle telemetry systems is monumentally daft. A modern Bugatti is essentially a 3,000,000-euro rolling satellite that snitches on its own driver every second.
Rimac and his engineers pulled up the server logs, watching live data for speed, coordinates, and fuel levels as the thief bolted toward Slovenia with an hour head start. Refusing to sit around eating popcorn while police filed paperwork, Rimac jumped into his personal Porsche 911, which conveniently had a full tank of gas, floored the throttle, and launched a private high-speed pursuit across Central Europe after his own hypercar.
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike Anyone who knows an 8.0-liter quad-turbocharged W16 knows its mortal enemy is not a spike strip, but fuel economy. A 100-liter, or 26-gallon, fuel tank isn't good for much if the sixteen-piston behemoth sips gas like it's free. Watching the fuel gauge plummet on the live telemetry feed, Rimac hoped the joyride would fizzle out at a Slovenian pump. Instead, our enterprising bandit pulled into a station, squeezed in half a tank of fuel, allegedly drove off without paying, and blasted across the border. Into Austria.
(That’s the one European country nobody should ever mess with. It’s happened in the past – twice. We all know how that ended).
Picture the sheer absurdity: a Croatian would-be job seeker fleeing toward Germany in a stolen three-million-euro hypercar running on half a tank of pilfered unleaded. By then, Croatian, Slovenian, and Austrian police forces had joined the chase, with one Austrian officer added directly into the Rimac team’s group chat for live GPS drops. Shortly after 7:00 PM, Styrian motorway police boxed the Chiron in at a Seiersberg gas station.
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike When Rimac finally rolled up to the scene near Graz along the A9 Pyhrn motorway, he naively figured he would flash his driver’s license, shake a few hands, and drive his Bugatti home. Instead, he walked into a cinematic blockade featuring 10 police cruisers and an international task force of hot pursuit officers. Austrian bureaucracy does not care if your name is literally on the company building; the car was winched onto a flatbed truck. (I told you about them).
Here is where a hilarious pub yarn transforms into a deeply humane story. While stuck at the Styrian police station until the early morning hours proving ownership, Rimac asked to meet the culprit. Discovering a distressed 36-year-old struggling with a troubled past, Rimac felt genuine empathy rather than rage. He had even hoped to drive the bloke back home to his family, and he refused to press private charges.
(I have one question, though: Mate runs Bugatti. Exactly what proof of ownership were the police demanding from him, other than just the regular papers?)
Photo: YouTube/Automotive Mike Of course, cross-border grand theft auto of a 3,000,000-euro asset triggers automatic prosecution in both Austria and Croatia, though prosecutors released the perpetrator to defend himself at liberty. The Chiron suffered minor cosmetic damage that Molsheim’s artisans will easily buff out, and everyone walked away unharmed.
Rimac still refuses to build fences around his campus, though he finally promised to keep the keys in his pocket from now on. Or, in any case, to not leave them in the car. I wonder if that job hunt still stands, and if the culprit would get a second chance at that interview. source_document.body:
Amazon reported record operating profitability in the third quarter on Thursday after the market closed, as the e-commerce giant continued expanding its delivery network and robotics investments amid higher transportation costs.
CEO Andy Jassy said investments in same-day fulfillment facilities and ultra-fast delivery services are helping the company attract more customers while lowering fulfillment expenditures.
“We’re on track to reduce cost to serve per unit for the fourth consecutive year,” Jassy said during a call with analysts.
The Seattle-based company reported third-quarter revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12% from $180.2 billion a year earlier. Operating income surged 61% to $28.1 billion, compared with $17.4 billion in the same period last year.
Revenue in the quarter came in below Wall Street estimates of $202.3 billion, while earnings per share came in at $1.89, lower than the expectation of $1.96.
Amazon’s (Nasdaq: AMZN ) operating margin reached 13.9%, its highest ever, as improvements across its retail and cloud computing businesses helped offset higher expenses.
“In our fulfillment network, the team navigated higher transportation costs from fuel inflation and higher line haul rates,” Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky said.
Despite those pressures, Amazon lowered its overall cost to serve during the quarter through better inventory placement, shorter shipping distances and package consolidation, he said.
Shipping costs increased 11% year over year, compared with 12% growth in units shipped. Excluding fuel and linehaul inflation, shipping costs rose 8%, approximately 4 percentage points slower than unit growth.
Amazon’s North America segment, which includes its U.S. and Canadian retail operations, generated $112.9 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 6% year over year.
Operating income in the segment jumped to $8.7 billion from $4.8 billion a year earlier, an increase of approximately 81%.
North America’s operating margin reached 7.7%.
International revenue increased 5% to $43.1 billion, while operating income climbed to $1.6 billion from $1.2 billion.
Amazon said the timing of Prime Day affected year-over-year comparisons because the shopping event occurred in the second quarter of 2026 for most major markets, compared with the third quarter in 2025.
Excluding that timing change, Amazon estimated third-quarter revenue growth would have been approximately 4 percentage points higher.
Amazon said it achieved its fastest third-quarter delivery speeds ever for Prime members, delivering more than 1.5 billion items on the same day or overnight during the three-month period ending Sept. 30.
Automation remains a major component of Amazon’s strategy to lower fulfillment expenses and increase productivity.
Jassy told analysts the company now operates more than 1 million robots across its fulfillment network.
He said robotics has contributed to improved productivity, reduced operating costs and record-low safety incident levels across its fulfillment operations.
Amazon doubled its fleet of robotic arms, including Cardinal and Sparrow systems, during 2026, according to Olsavsky.
The company is also developing robotics foundation models designed to help machines perform increasingly complex physical tasks.
During the question-and-answer portion of Thursday’s earnings call, Jassy said that transportation cost pressures are expected to continue into the fourth quarter.
Responding to an analyst’s question about fuel and linehaul inflation, Jassy said the impact would be somewhat higher in the fourth quarter than in the third.
Amazon implemented a fuel surcharge earlier this year for sellers using its Fulfillment by Amazon service, allowing the company to recover some of its higher fuel expenses.
However, Jassy said the surcharge does not fully offset the increases, leaving Amazon exposed to higher costs for inbound retail shipments and outbound deliveries.
Amazon expects fourth-quarter net sales between $240 billion and $247 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 12% to 16%.
The company forecast fourth-quarter operating income between $28.5 billion and $33.5 billion, compared with $25 billion in the year-earlier period.

2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Dodge Charger Gets Special-Edition Package Celebrating 90 Years of Mopar
Audi R8 vs. Nissan GT-R Drag Race Is Over in 8 Seconds – Video
6 photos
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | Wheels Plus
Discontinued cars are definitely not dead, especially if they are on the cool side of their classes, and this definitely applies to the Audi R8 and the Nissan GT-R, because both were dropped, in case you forgot.
Believe it or not, it’s been more than a year since the last Godzilla rolled off the assembly line at the Kaminokawa factory in Tochigi, Japan. That happened in August 2025, and this model lived a very long and fruitful life, as it entered production back in December 2007. Over the years, the company constantly refined it, and regardless of the configuration, the same twin-turbocharged V6 engine remained under the hood, with its 3.8-liter displacement, driving all four wheels through a dual-clutch six-speed automatic transmission.
The original Nissan GT-R (R35) had 473 horsepower (480 ps/353 kW) to play with, and while that may not be anything to write home about these days, it made it a proper Porsche 911 Carrera fighter back then. Subsequently, the lump was upgraded to 478 hp (485 ps/357 kW), and then to 523 hp (530 ps/390 kW). Mid-range model year cars came with 542 hp (550 ps/405 kW) and 562 hp (570 ps/419 kW), whereas the range-toppers had 592 hp (600 ps/441 kW) available via the right pedal.
According to various tests, the final Nissan GT-R Nismo could reach 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill in less than three seconds, and it is definitely worth noting that some examples completed the sprint in two and a half seconds. Flat-out, it exceeded 205 mph (315 kph), so it was definitely a supercar dressed as an aging sports model. As for the standing quarter mile, it took a little over 10 seconds, with an exit speed of around 138 mph (222 kph), and that is definitely impressive, isn’t it?
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | Wheels Plus As for the Audi R8 , it too is dead and buried. The second-generation left the assembly line at the Heilbronn facility in Germany for good at the end of 2024, after hitting it ten years before. Unlike its ad-hoc rival mentioned above, this model was also offered as a two-door convertible (Spyder) in addition to the regular two-door coupe, and all versions featured a longitudinal mid-engine layout, and either rear-wheel drive or all-wheel drive, depending on the configuration.
Audi’s second-generation R8 shared its nuts and bolts with the Lamborghini Huracan, whereas its predecessor was based on the same platform as the Gallardo. The powertrain of choice was a 5.2-liter naturally aspirated V10, just like the Temerario’s predecessor, and in its top form, the engine was officially good for well over 600 horsepower, allowing the R8 to hit 60 mph (97 kph) in roughly three seconds, and allowing it to complete the standing quarter mile in just over 10.5 seconds, with an exit speed of almost 135 mph (217 mph).
Therefore, the Nissan GT-R and the Audi R8 are capable of pulling similar numbers, but have you ever seen them engage in a quarter mile battle from a standing start? That would obviously be a yes, as these two models met at various drag strips and drag events worldwide over the years, and will continue to do so. Some of them have been visited by the tuning fairy, but the majority remains stock.
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | Wheels Plus But what about the ones depicted on video below? Well, as you already know, none of them is capable of completing the standing 1/4-mile in eight seconds, not without some serious outside intervention, so the answer is yes. Yes, they have been visited by the tuning fairy. As a result, they are extremely fast, to the point where they can punch a class above their weight. Well, at least the winner is, because the loser should have definitely stayed home.
The footage was recently shared on YouTube by Wheels Plus, and was shot at the Bradenton Motorsports Park in Florida. The video in question is a little over one minute long, and shows the two engage in a standing quarter-mile brawl that concluded a few seconds later. That’s because the winner crossed the finish line in just 8.88 seconds, with an exit speed of over 165 mph (265 kph), whereas the loser did it in 10.21 seconds. And that’s some 1.4 seconds slower in case you are keeping track of the numbers.
Now, trying to figure out which of the two was faster on that day is anything but easy, because it could have gone either way. Nevertheless, if your life depended on it, and you had to pick a winner before watching the footage, which one would it be? Do you think the Audi R8 completed the standing quarter mile faster than the Nissan GT-R, or was it the either way around? This would be a good time to place a little bet, as you are about to find out which of these was quicker.

The nation’s largest less-than-truckload carrier, FedEx Freight, said Thursday that volumes have continued to stabilize and that it expects to see stronger operating leverage next year as a standalone company. Its local, dedicated LTL sales teams are seeing business wins and driving a better freight mix across the network.
FedEx Freight ( NYSE: FDXF ) completed its spinoff from FedEx ( NYSE: FDX ) in June. FedEx reported financial results on Wednesday.
The carrier reported four-month results (June through September) Thursday after the market closed as part of a transition to calendar-year financial reporting.
Revenue in the period increased 9% year over year to $3.28 billion. Revenue per day was up 8%. Adjusted earnings per share of $2.15 were 70 cents lower y/y.
Table: FedEx Freight’s key performance indicators
The revenue increase was driven by a 9% increase in revenue per hundredweight (yield), while tonnage was level with the prior-year period. The tonnage result stemmed from a 1% decline in shipments per day, which was offset by a 1% increase in weight per shipment.
Yield (ex-fuel) was up just 0.3% y/y. Revenue per shipment (ex-fuel) increased 2%.
It has repriced approximately 25% of its contract business since the separation and said net revenue churn has improved. It expects both volumes and yield (ex-fuel) to increase in the fourth quarter. September marked the ninth straight month of expansion for the U.S. manufacturing complex, which is a significant source of LTL freight.
FedEx Freight’s 2027 general rate increase is expected to average 6.9% and takes effect on Jan. 8.
The company reported an 84.5% adjusted operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ), which was 90 basis points better y/y.
Guidance for the fourth quarter includes revenue of $2.3 billion to $2.37 billion, a 13% y/y increase at the midpoint of the range. Higher diesel fuel surcharges will be a primary driver of the increase. Diesel prices were 48% higher y/y in the third quarter.
Adjusted operating income is expected to increase 20% y/y (at the midpoint) to a range of $185 million to $205 million. (The guide implies a 91.4% to 92% adjusted OR, 50 bps better y/y at the midpoint.)
The company said it will soon decide on a dividend, and on buying back stock. It said that share repurchases would likely be executed to offset dilution as FedEx unwinds its equity position.
Shares of FDXF were up 3% in after-hours trading on Thursday.
Why it matters? FedEx Freight’s standalone results provide deeper context around its LTL operations and broader market trends.

source_document.body:
By Nidhi Gupta, Founder & CEO, Portcast
30 October 2026
The most common misconception about AI in logistics is that it’s a magic button. If it were, the average operator’s day would look very different two years into the AI wave. But it doesn’t, and the portal-hopping, the chasing, the manual reconciling are mostly still there. That gap, between the noise about AI and the reality on the operations floor, is worth being honest about, because it shows where AI has created real value and where it’s still just noise.
First, AI is real in the boring work. It helps most when it takes repeatable, daily work off the operator. Freight runs on messy documents that aren’t designed for machines to read: the PDFs, rate sheets, and carrier contracts that come in every format, each with its own rules. AI is very good at reading that mess and turning it into something a tech system can act on. One shipper we worked with was receiving freight invoices from 9 different carriers in more than 100 formats. Even the same carrier office would send invoices in different formats. Once we read them automatically, 55% showed discrepancies against freight agreements and actual container movements. Finding these discrepancies with AI is where the real impact comes from. People are one of the biggest costs in a forwarding business, so every hour saved from manual reconciliation and every overcharge caught before it’s paid shows up directly on the P&L.
None of the AI use-cases work without clean data. Every forwarder I talk to already knows this, and most still underestimate it. A single shipment carries thousands of data points across operational, financial, and commercial files. If those are wrong, the AI still answers confidently, just wrongly, and you find out when your customer does. When I talk about data, I mean combining external data like shipment visibility, sailing schedules, service reliability, and tradelane risks with internal data like order-level information, contract terms, and customer SLAs. Once the data foundation is set up and clean, AI can produce insights and recommendations.
The other critical thing that separates the AI that adds value from the AI that fades a few weeks after launch is user adoption. A model can be good, but if the people meant to use it don’t understand or trust it, they will work around it and revert to their own spreadsheets and gut feeling. The AI that proves its value is the one operators reach for on their own because it fits how they already work.
And finally, when we talk about AI, it’s human-in-the-loop, instead of fully automated. Freight is complex, and there are real legal and financial consequences when something goes wrong. For anything that touches a customer or the P&L, a person stays in the loop, reviews the AI’s recommendation, and makes the final call. The model that works is hybrid: the AI does the scanning and drafting; the operator keeps the judgment. In a business this complex, that is the one worth continuing, at least in the near term.
That’s the test behind our three AI agents at Portcast : each one has to save real time or cut real cost, which is why there are three concrete ones, not a hundred agents.
The Daily Agent reviews every shipment overnight and hands each operator one ranked brief of what changed, what needs a decision, and where demurrage is building. It cuts morning triage from about 45 minutes to 10, roughly 152 hours a year per operator, and because it catches demurrage while the free time is still on the clock, it reduces costs before they occur.
Take the booking decision. Every booking makes an operator weigh many conflicting data points at once to choose what’s right for the customer and what’s right for the business, and at scale, that’s almost impossible to do well. So, operators fall back on habit, and the call ends up based on a guess rather than the data. Our Route Planning Agent handles that decision across what matters: schedule reliability, price, allocation agreements, and live disruptions, and the operator decides which counts most. You get a process that scales, with customers booked on the services that fit their priorities, and steadier service because of it.
The Market Reliability Agent turns months of carrier performance into string-level evidence, including transshipment services, not just the port pair. Two services on the same port pair can behave completely differently. Teams use it to negotiate tenders and move volume to the carriers that actually deliver, and to price premium services on real performance rather than carrier claims. That is the cost taken out on the buy side and margin protected on the sell side. All three show their work, and none act without a person’s sign-off.
I also believe that not everything needs AI. If you can solve a problem with a clear set of rules and inputs, there is value in keeping it deterministic rather than adding AI simply because you can.
So, is AI a magic button? No. It’s a tool, and it is valuable when it clears real work off the desk and gives you back time or cuts costs, with a person still making the decisions that matter. If you’re running an AI pilot right now, ask one question: what will my operators stop doing on Monday because of this?
